newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: More Portuguese repo rate cuts seen this year.
newsitem.headline: More Portuguese repo rate cuts seen this year.

text.p: Portuguese key rate cuts announced on Monday open the way for further cuts in the repo rate in 1996 as the spread between the repo rate and the draining rate, used to absorb excess liquidity, has widened to 50 basis points, analysts said.
"This spread of rate cuts opens the way for further cuts in the repo rate," said an operator with a foreign bank in Lisbon, who asked not to be identified.
"I would not be surprised if the repo rate eased a further 15 basis points this year," he added.
The Bank of Portugal said it cut its repurchase rate 10 basis points (bp) to 6.90 percent and the draining rate 40 bp to 6.40 percent, effective Tuesday.
The central bank also cut its emergency lending rate by half a point to 8.50 percent, effective Tuesday, the start of a new seven-day commercial bank reserve period.
Portuguese bonds, which had anticipated the rate cuts, traded at all-time highs on Monday, dealers said.
"The Bank of Portugal has followed a tradition of making a large cut in the draining rate so that cuts in the repo rate can follow," said another dealer.
The timing of further repo rate cuts will depend on progress to control inflation, the approval of the 1997 budget and the outcome of 1997 public sector wage talks, analysts said.
"Further repo rate cuts will depend on inflation numbers, approval of the budget and an encouraging outcome of the public sector wage round," said Isabel Cabral of Lisbon broker Fincor.

The government's 1997 budget proposals, now being discussed in fine detail by parliament, keep a tight lid on spending and forecast a strong boost to revenues to meet the tough entry test for joining the European single currency in January 1999.
The budget is expected to be passed by parliament in a final vote on December 11.
Analysts said a key reason for the rate cuts announced on Monday was the good inflation news for October.

"Inflation was a determining factor in today's decision and makes room for further rate cuts, which shows that the Bank of Portugal does not fear a resurgence of inflation for now," said another analyst with a bank, who asked not to be identified.

In October, inflation dipped 0.1 percent month-on-month, which brought the year-on-year rate to three percent. The 12-month rolling average, the government's benchmark, slipped to 3.2 percent from 3.3 percent in September.
